The Gulf killifish Fundulus grandis is a common cyprinodontiform species inhabiting salt marshes and estuaries along the Gulf coast of North America. Neonates emerge as prolarvae following the completion of yolk-sac absorption, with newly hatched individuals exhibiting a remarkably small body mass of just 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams]. This minimal wet weight at birth reflects the modest egg diameter of approximately two millimeters, which yields a spherical volume conducive to rapid development in warm, shallow nursery habitats. As the yolk-dependent larva transitions to exogenous feeding, growth proceeds steadily under favorable thermal regimes, allowing juveniles to increase in mass and length before the onset of gonadal recrudescence. The population attains sexual maturation at a threshold wet weight of approximately 7 grams [Wwp = approximately 7 grams], a value consistent with the onset of vitellogenesis and spermiation in captive-reared cohorts. Puberty is therefore tied more closely to the attainment of a critical body size rather than a strict chronological age, a pattern observed widely among small-bodied estuarine teleosts.

Reproductive output in Fundulus grandis is strongly influenced by ambient water temperature, which modulates both spawning frequency and the number of oocytes released per event. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 26.5 °C [T = 26.5 °C], females achieve a daily reproduction rate corresponding to approximately 35 eggs per day, with a spawning event producing approximately 35 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 35 eggs per clutch] and sustaining approximately 35 spawning events per year [F_R_i = approximately 35 spawning events per year] during the peak breeding season. This maximum annual output of roughly 12858 eggs per female reflects a modest fecundity typical of fundulid species that invest in relatively large, yolky eggs. The thermal dependence of gametogenesis means that seasonal fluctuations in marsh temperature can delay or compress the spawning window, with cooler springs reducing the number of viable clutches deposited. Field surveys of gravid females collected from tidal creeks corroborate these laboratory findings.

The ultimate total length recorded for this species in wild populations is 18 centimeters [Li = 18 centimeters], a value that marks the upper boundary of somatic growth for both sexes. Males and females rarely exceed this asymptotic length, although coastal populations subject to reduced predation pressure have occasionally produced individuals approaching 19 centimeters. Morphometric data collected from museum specimen series indicate that the corresponding ultimate wet weight is approximately 44.3 grams [Wwi = approximately 44.3 grams], a mass that reflects the robust body depth and compressed morphology characteristic of adult killifish. This relationship between length and mass follows a positive allometric scaling exponent derived from a large sample of adults, confirming that weight increases more rapidly than length as fish approach their maximum size. Seasonal variation in body condition can cause adults to fluctuate below this asymptotic mass during periods of intense reproductive activity or food limitation, but post-spawning recovery typically restores mass to values near the ultimate benchmark within several weeks.

Longevity in Gulf killifish is constrained by the energetic demands of reproduction and the episodic stressors of marsh life, including hypoxia, temperature extremes, and episodic predation. The maximum recorded lifespan from birth in wild individuals, measured under thermal conditions averaging 22.5 °C [T = 22.5 °C], is 3 years [am = 3 years]. This relatively short time since birth at death aligns with the species' strategy of rapid maturation and high annual reproductive investment, which trades extended somatic persistence against early and repeated breeding. Senescent individuals collected during late summer often exhibit frayed fins, reduced gonadosomatic indices, and diminished escape responses, signaling the physiological deterioration that precedes natural mortality. Captive cohorts maintained at stable temperatures slightly below 22.5 °C have occasionally survived beyond 3 years [am = 3 years], suggesting that cooler conditions may modestly extend lifespan by slowing metabolic wear at a temperature of 22.5 °C [T = 22.5 °C]. Nonetheless, 3 years [am = 3 years] remains the benchmark for maximum longevity under naturally fluctuating field conditions at a temperature of 22.5 °C [T = 22.5 °C].

Ecologically, Fundulus grandis occupies a pivotal trophic position in salt marsh food webs, serving as both a consumer of benthic invertebrates and a prey item for piscivorous birds and larger fish. The species' capacity to tolerate salinities ranging from nearly fresh water to hypersaline conditions allows it to exploit habitat patches that are inaccessible to less euryhaline competitors. Spawning occurs primarily during the spring and early summer months, with adhesive demersal eggs deposited onto submerged vegetation or shell hash in shallow tidal creeks. The chorionate embryos undergo rapid development, with eclosion occurring within approximately two weeks at temperatures near 26.5 °C [T = 26.5 °C], a rate that synchronizes larval emergence with peak zooplankton abundance. Population genetic studies reveal moderate connectivity among estuaries, though localized adaptation to thermal and salinity regimes is evident in clinal variation at several metabolic loci. The remarkable physiological plasticity of this species continues to make it a model organism for studies of environmental stress tolerance in fishes.
